name: Sautéing
definition: Cooking food quickly in a small amount of fat over high heat.
how_to: Heat a pan over medium-high to high heat.
Add a small amount of fat (oil, butter).
When the fat is hot, add the food.
Toss or stir constantly to prevent burning and ensure even cooking.
why_its_done: To brown food, develop complex flavors through the Maillard reaction, and cook quickly while retaining moisture.
common_mistakes: Overcrowding the pan (causes steaming instead of sautéing)
Not heating the pan/oil enough before adding food
Using the wrong oil (one with a low smoke point)

name: Stir-Frying
definition: A Chinese cooking technique in which ingredients are fried in a small amount of very hot oil while being stirred or tossed in a wok.
how_to: Preheat a wok or large pan until smoking hot.
Add a high smoke point oil.
Add aromatics, then protein, then vegetables in order of cooking time.
Toss continuously until cooked.
why_its_done: To cook food extremely fast, preserving color, texture, and nutritional value.
common_mistakes: Adding wet ingredients to the hot oil
Not prepping all ingredients beforehand (mise en place)
Using too much sauce, turning it into a boil

name: Braising
definition: A combination cooking method that uses both wet and dry heats: typically, the food is first seared at a high temperature, then finished in a covered pot at a lower temperature while sitting in some amount of liquid.
how_to: Dry the meat and season well.
Sear the meat in hot fat until browned on all sides.
Remove meat, sauté aromatics, and deglaze the pot.
Return meat, add liquid (stock, wine) halfway up the meat.
Cover and simmer low and slow (stovetop or oven) until fork-tender.
why_its_done: To break down tough connective tissues in cuts of meat, transforming them into gelatin for a rich, tender result.
common_mistakes: Using too much liquid (boiling instead of braising)
Cooking at too high a temperature
Skipping the initial searing step

name: Blanching
definition: Scalding vegetables in boiling water or oil, usually briefly, and then immediately moving them to an ice bath to halt the cooking process.
how_to: Bring a large pot of heavily salted water to a rolling boil.
Submerge the vegetables for 1-3 minutes.
Remove vegetables with a slotted spoon.
Plunge immediately into a bowl of ice water.
why_its_done: To soften vegetables, set their vibrant color, loosen skins for peeling, or prepare them for freezing by deactivating enzymes.
common_mistakes: Not using enough salt in the boiling water
Skipping or delaying the ice bath (shocking)
Overcooking the vegetables

name: Steaming
definition: Cooking food using the steam from boiling water without submerging the food in the water itself.
how_to: Bring an inch or two of water to a boil in a pot.
Place food in a steamer basket above the water.
Cover tightly to trap the steam and cook until tender.
why_its_done: To cook delicately without agitating the food or leaching out water-soluble nutrients.
common_mistakes: Letting the water touch the food
Running out of water in the pot (dry boiling)
Opening the lid too often, losing steam

name: Poaching
definition: Gently cooking food submerged in liquid at a low temperature, typically between 160°F and 180°F (71°C to 82°C).
how_to: Heat liquid (water, broth, wine) until a few bubbles gently rise to the surface.
Submerge the food carefully.
Maintain the low heat and cook until done.
why_its_done: To cook delicate proteins without toughening them, keeping them moist.
common_mistakes: Letting the liquid boil, which toughens the protein
Not flavoring the poaching liquid

name: Simmering
definition: Cooking food in liquid at a temperature just below boiling (around 185°F to 205°F).
how_to: Bring liquid to a boil.
Reduce heat until bubbles gently and occasionally break the surface.
Add food and maintain the temperature.
why_its_done: To meld flavors in soups and stews, or cook foods gently over time.
common_mistakes: Allowing it to reach a rapid boil
Covering tightly and accidentally boiling over

name: Deep-Frying
definition: Cooking food by completely submerging it in hot fat or oil.
how_to: Heat oil to specific temp (usually 350-375°F).
Carefully drop dry or battered food into the oil.
Cook until golden brown.
Remove and drain on a wire rack or paper towels.
why_its_done: To create a crisp exterior while cooking the interior quickly through high heat conduction.
common_mistakes: Frying at too low a temperature (greasy food)
Overcrowding the pot (drops oil temp drastically)
Not drying food before frying (causes dangerous splatters)

name: Shallow Frying
definition: Cooking food in a pan with enough oil to reach about halfway up the sides of the food.
how_to: Heat oil in a heavy skillet until shimmering.
Add breaded or battered food.
Cook until the bottom is crispy and golden, then carefully flip.
Drain excess oil.
why_its_done: To achieve a crispy crust on flatter items without using a massive volume of oil.
common_mistakes: Flipping too early before a crust forms
Using oil with a low smoke point

name: Tempering
definition: Slowly raising the temperature of a delicate ingredient (like eggs or chocolate) or blooming spices in hot oil to release flavors.
how_to: For eggs: Slowly whisk a small amount of hot liquid into the cold eggs to warm them gently.
For spices (Tadka): Heat oil or ghee, add whole spices until they sizzle and become fragrant.
why_its_done: To prevent eggs from scrambling in hot soup/sauce, or to extract fat-soluble flavors from spices.
common_mistakes: Adding hot liquid to eggs too quickly
Burning spices in too hot oil

name: Double Boiling
definition: Using indirect heat to gently cook or melt ingredients.
how_to: Bring an inch of water to a simmer in a saucepan.
Place a heatproof bowl snugly over the pot, ensuring the bottom doesn't touch the water.
Add ingredients to the bowl to melt or cook.
why_its_done: To provide gentle, even heat for heat-sensitive ingredients that might burn or separate over direct flame.
common_mistakes: Letting the water touch the bottom of the bowl
Getting water droplets into melting chocolate (causing seizing)

name: Bain-Marie
definition: A water bath used in an oven to provide gentle, uniform heat.
how_to: Place a baking dish containing the food into a larger roasting pan.
Pour boiling water into the larger pan until it reaches halfway up the sides of the inner dish.
Bake as directed.
why_its_done: To prevent the edges of custards or delicate baked goods from overcooking before the center sets, and to prevent cracking.
common_mistakes: Splashing water into the food
Using cold water instead of boiling water

name: Deglazing
definition: Adding liquid to a hot pan to loosen browned bits of food stuck to the bottom.
how_to: Remove cooked meat/vegetables from the pan.
Pour in a liquid (wine, broth, vinegar, water).
Use a wooden spoon to scrape the flavorful browned bits (fond) from the bottom as the liquid bubbles.
why_its_done: To capture the intense flavor of the fond to make a pan sauce or gravy.
common_mistakes: Deglazing a pan with burnt (blackened) fond, which will taste bitter
Using an unsafe liquid over open flame without turning heat off first (e.g., strong alcohol)

name: Reduction
definition: Simmering or boiling a liquid to evaporate water and concentrate its flavors and thicken its consistency.
how_to: Place liquid (sauce, stock, wine) in an uncovered pan.
Simmer until the volume decreases to the desired amount (e.g., 'reduce by half').
why_its_done: To intensify flavor and create a thicker, more syrupy texture without adding starches.
common_mistakes: Boiling too rapidly, which can turn the sauce bitter or break an emulsion
Reducing a liquid that is already too salty

name: Emulsification
definition: Forcing two unmixable liquids (like oil and water/vinegar) to combine into a stable mixture.
how_to: Start with the water-based ingredient (and an emulsifier like mustard or egg yolk).
Whisk vigorously.
Slowly, drop by drop, drizzle in the oil while continuing to whisk until the mixture thickens and comes together.
why_its_done: To create creamy, cohesive dressings and sauces from oil and acidic liquids.
common_mistakes: Adding oil too quickly, causing the mixture to break (separate)
Not using an emulsifier

name: Marinating
definition: Soaking food in a seasoned, often acidic or enzymatic liquid before cooking.
how_to: Combine acid, oil, aromatics, and salt to make the marinade.
Submerge the protein or vegetable in the marinade.
Refrigerate for the appropriate time (30 mins for seafood, up to 24h for tough meats).
why_its_done: To add flavor and slightly tenderize proteins.
common_mistakes: Marinating too long in highly acidic mixtures (turns meat mushy)
Reusing marinade that touched raw meat without boiling it first

name: Fermentation
definition: The breakdown of carbohydrates by bacteria and yeast to produce acids, alcohol, or gases.
how_to: Introduce beneficial bacteria/yeast to food.
Keep in a controlled environment (often anaerobic and at room temperature) for days or weeks.
why_its_done: To preserve food, improve digestibility, and develop complex, tangy, umami flavors.
common_mistakes: Using insufficient salt, allowing bad bacteria to grow
Exposing anaerobic ferments to oxygen (causes mold)

name: Proofing
definition: The final rise of shaped yeast dough before baking.
how_to: Shape the kneaded dough.
Place in a warm, draft-free environment.
Cover to prevent drying out and leave until doubled in size.
why_its_done: To allow yeast to produce carbon dioxide gas, creating the airy, open crumb structure in bread.
common_mistakes: Overproofing (dough collapses when touched or baked)
Underproofing (results in dense, heavy bread)

name: Kneading
definition: Working dough by hand or mixer to develop the gluten network.
how_to: Push the dough away with the heel of your hand.
Fold it back over itself.
Turn 90 degrees and repeat until smooth and elastic.
why_its_done: To align gluten proteins, giving dough the strength and structure needed to trap gas and rise.
common_mistakes: Over-kneading in a mixer (dough becomes tough or breaks down)
Under-kneading (bread won't rise properly)

name: Folding
definition: Gently combining a light, airy ingredient (like whipped egg whites) with a heavier mixture.
how_to: Add a portion of the light mixture into the heavy mixture.
Use a spatula to cut down through the center, scrape across the bottom, and bring the heavy mixture up over the light mixture.
Rotate the bowl and repeat gently until just combined.
why_its_done: To mix ingredients without deflating the trapped air.
common_mistakes: Stirring vigorously instead of folding, which knocks out the air
Folding too long

name: Creaming
definition: Beating solid fat (usually butter) and sugar together until light, fluffy, and pale.
how_to: Ensure butter is at room temperature.
Beat with sugar using a mixer on medium speed for 3-5 minutes.
Scrape down the bowl occasionally.
why_its_done: To trap air bubbles in the fat, which provides physical leavening and tenderness to baked goods.
common_mistakes: Using butter that is too cold (won't trap air) or too warm/melted (collapses)
Not creaming long enough

name: Caramelization
definition: The browning of sugar, a process used extensively in cooking for the resulting sweet nutty flavor and brown color.
how_to: Heat sugar (or naturally sugary foods like onions) slowly over medium-low heat.
Cook until the natural sugars melt and turn amber/brown, taking care not to burn.
why_its_done: To transform simple sweetness into complex, nutty, buttery, and slightly bitter flavors.
common_mistakes: Cooking too fast or walking away, causing it to burn (turns bitter instantly)
Stirring wet caramel too much, causing crystallization

name: Roasting
definition: Cooking food in an oven using dry, indirect heat, usually at a higher temperature (400°F+).
how_to: Toss food in oil and seasonings.
Spread evenly on a baking sheet, ensuring space between items.
Cook uncovered in a hot oven until browned and tender.
why_its_done: To caramelize the exterior and cook the interior evenly, enhancing natural sweetness and savory notes.
common_mistakes: Overcrowding the pan (causes steaming instead of roasting)
Not using enough oil

name: Grilling
definition: Cooking food rapidly over direct, radiant heat, usually on a grate over hot coals or gas flames.
how_to: Preheat grill until very hot.
Oil the grates.
Place food directly over the heat for searing, or move to indirect heat to finish cooking without burning.
why_its_done: To give food a distinct smoky flavor and charred exterior.
common_mistakes: Constantly flipping or moving the food
Cooking thick cuts purely on direct high heat (burnt outside, raw inside)

name: Smoking
definition: Flavoring, browning, or cooking food by exposing it to smoke from smoldering wood or other materials.
how_to: Maintain a low, steady temperature (usually 225°F-250°F) in a smoker.
Add hardwood chips or logs to generate smoke.
Cook meat very slowly over several hours.
why_its_done: To impart a deep, woodsy flavor and slowly break down extremely tough cuts of meat (like brisket or ribs) into tender masterpieces.
common_mistakes: Using softwoods (pine), which give off toxic, bad-tasting smoke
Too much smoke ('dirty smoke'), making food taste bitter

name: Pressure Cooking
definition: Cooking food in a sealed vessel that does not permit air or liquids to escape below a preset pressure.
how_to: Add food and liquid to the pressure cooker.
Seal the lid and heat until high pressure is achieved.
Cook for the specified time, then release pressure quickly or naturally depending on the food.
why_its_done: To drastically reduce cooking times (up to 70% faster) and extract flavor quickly.
common_mistakes: Overfilling the cooker above the max fill line
Not using enough liquid to build steam/pressure
Forcing the lid open before pressure is released (extremely dangerous)

name: Sous-Vide
definition: Cooking food vacuum-sealed in a plastic bag in a precisely regulated water bath.
how_to: Season food and seal in a vacuum bag.
Submerge in a water bath heated by an immersion circulator to the exact desired final temperature of the food.
Cook for hours; remove and sear quickly before serving.
why_its_done: To achieve absolute precision and perfection in doneness, with zero risk of overcooking.
common_mistakes: Not searing the food afterward (food looks grey and unappetizing)
Not removing all air from the bag (bag floats, causing uneven cooking)

name: Searing
definition: Cooking the surface of food (usually meat) at high temperature until a browned crust forms.
how_to: Pat the meat completely dry.
Heat a heavy skillet (like cast iron) until very hot.
Add oil, then the meat. Do not move the meat until a crust forms.
Flip and repeat.
why_its_done: To build massive flavor through the Maillard reaction. (Myth buster: Searing does NOT 'lock in juices', it only builds flavor/texture).
common_mistakes: Trying to sear wet meat (it will steam instead)
Moving the meat too soon, tearing the crust
Overcrowding the pan

name: Baking
definition: Cooking food using prolonged dry heat acting by convection, normally in an oven.
how_to: Preheat the oven to the specified temperature.
Place prepared food in a baking dish or sheet.
Cook in the center of the oven until done.
why_its_done: To create structure in doughs/batters, or to gently cook items without direct intense heat.
common_mistakes: Not preheating the oven fully
Opening the oven door too often, dropping the temperature
Using dark vs light baking pans incorrectly (dark pans cook edges faster)

name: Broiling
definition: Cooking by exposing food to direct radiant heat, either on a grill over live coals or below a gas burner or electric coil in an oven.
how_to: Preheat the broiler.
Place food on a broiler pan to catch fat.
Place close to the heat source (usually 2-4 inches away).
Watch constantly as food burns quickly.
why_its_done: To quickly cook thin cuts of meat, melt cheese, or char the skin of vegetables.
common_mistakes: Walking away (broiling goes from perfect to burnt in seconds)
Using glass bakeware under a broiler (it will shatter)
used_in: melting cheese on french onion soup
